text.what: A locket on a neckchain: a round hollow pouch with something shut inside it, usually a phallus. What it was made of tracked the family's money — gold or gold foil at the top, lead, leather or cloth further down. It was given to a freeborn Roman boy nine days after he was born and he wore it until he stopped being a boy.
text.story:
The bulla has an end date built into it. Before a young man put on the toga virilis, the toga of manhood, he handed his boyhood bulla to the household's Lares, the family's own gods, and it stayed with them. The girls' version, the lunula, came off on the eve of a wedding, together with her childhood toys.

Who could wear one was not open. The bulla marks a freeborn Roman boy and a Roman citizen in the making; the object and the status are the same statement. Some modern readers take a single line in Macrobius about an amulet worn by a general in his triumph as evidence that the childhood bulla was also standard triumphal regalia. The cited account reports that reading without endorsing it, and so does this record.

*Tradition holds —* the amulet inside was usually a phallus, a shape the cited account calls a bringer of good luck in antiquity. The container is the interesting part. The protection is real enough to be worth wearing and private enough to be shut in a case: nobody is meant to see what is working.

Ireland has bullae too, and they are not these. A small number of Late Bronze Age objects, roughly 1150 to 750 BCE, are called bullae because they look like the Roman ones — base metal or clay under a folded-over sheet of gold foil, incised with geometry, hung round the neck by a cord through a hole below the flat top. Whether they were ornament, amulet or something else is unclear, and that is why Ireland does not appear in this record's country list.

dating.label: Roman antiquity
dating.note: The cited article gives no attestation range for the Roman bulla. Its dated anchors are Plautus in the 3rd–2nd century BCE and Macrobius around 400 CE. The Irish bullae, a separate class, are dated in the article to about 1150–750 BCE.

object.note: The amulet inside is the working part; the bulla is the container. No published measurement was read.
